content.p: On the afternoon of Thursday 10 June 1971, a column of some 10,000 students set out from the Casco de Santo Tomás, a campus of the National Polytechnic Institute in Mexico City, to march to the Zócalo. It was the first large student street protest since the army and police fired on demonstrators at Tlatelolco in October 1968. Within a kilometre or so, young men in civilian clothes, armed with bamboo staves and then with firearms, fell on the marchers while uniformed police stood by. The attackers were the Halcones, the "Hawks", a paramilitary force that the Federal District government had recruited, paid and trained.

The death toll has never been settled. An early official figure was 11; the National Security Archive in Washington wrote of some 25 dead; the BBC's Spanish-language service put it near 30; and other Mexican outlets repeat an estimate of about 120. The government of President Luis Echeverría first denied that the Halcones existed. No one has been convicted. In 2021 President Andrés Manuel López Obrador apologised on behalf of the state.
content.h2: A march after the long silence
content.p: Echeverría took office on 1 December 1970. He had been interior secretary when Tlatelolco happened, but as president he promised an opening towards young people and respect for university independence, according to the National Security Archive. La Izquierda Diario adds that exiled student leaders were allowed back and some political prisoners freed.

The trigger for the march was in the northern city of Monterrey. After the state congress changed the bylaws of the Autonomous University of Nuevo León and cut its autonomy, students shut the university on 1 May. The governor, Eduardo Elizondo, sent police onto the campus. Echeverría then intervened to annul the law, and Elizondo resigned. A new university law took effect on 5 June, according to La Izquierda Diario. Even so, students at the IPN and UNAM kept the date they had called for 10 June. Their demands, as listed by Sopitas and La Izquierda Diario, went beyond Monterrey and included democratisation of teaching, a university budget equal to 12 per cent of gross domestic product, and an end to government repression.

The march mattered symbolically, the historian Camilo Vicente Ovalle told BBC Mundo. After 1968, taking the streets again meant taking back something that had been seized from them. He added that the march was unauthorised, and that the students found streets blocked by riot police.

Mexican reporting differs on where the Halcones came from. Milenio, citing reports of the former federal security agency held in the General Archive of the Nation, says the group appeared in 1968 as a government answer to youth movements, and names the then head of the Federal District Department, Alfonso Corona del Rosal, as its creator. Alfonso Martínez Domínguez, who governed the capital in 1970 and 1971, said in a 1998 interview that the Halcones were formed under Gustavo Díaz Ordaz and kept on under Echeverría, and that his administration only paid them while command lay with the Presidential General Staff. The U.S. embassy told Washington that the group had been founded in September 1968 to control leftist and anti-government students.

Several accounts agree on the man who ran them. Colonel Manuel Díaz Escobar Figueroa was deputy director of General Services in the Federal District Department. Milenio, citing the archive's reports, says he was chiefly responsible for their training; the UNAM's Gaceta describes the Halcones as organised and financed by the state under his direction, with advice from army officers and help from police and riot units. El Universal, quoting the researcher Jacinto Rodríguez Munguía, says recruits came from poor, violent neighbourhoods of the capital along with soldiers, and learned martial arts including kendo, which explains the bamboo sticks. Milenio puts their strength by 1971 at about a thousand members, mostly aged 18 to 25, paid an average of 60 pesos, with the Federal District Department supplying fuel and transport. A U.S. embassy cable of January 1971 gave an estimate of about 2,000 and said the Halcones had broken up a student rally on 4 November 1970 with bamboo sticks.

The same declassified cables show an American link. In January 1971 Foreign Secretary Emilio Rabasa asked Ambassador Robert McBride for police training in the United States for a Mexican group, and Díaz Escobar was named its coordinator. The embassy noted that he led the Halcones and warned that the men might be used "to play some role in the Halcones", according to the archive's quotation of the cable. Washington agreed to go ahead anyway. The first five trainees, among them the colonel's son, left for Washington on 8 March and were due home on 9 July, so none took part in the events of June.

Accounts of the timing differ slightly. BBC Mundo says the march began at 4 p.m.; the National Security Archive says the attack came at five. The route was meant to follow Avenida de los Maestros to the Mexico-Tacuba causeway. Félix Hernández, a student leader of the time, told the news agency Notimex that the government chose not to use uniformed troops and instead used the Halcones, who he said were former or serving soldiers. The Mexico Solidarity Media piece, which reprints a column from La Jornada, says riot police let the column pass after the students sang the national anthem, and calls that a trap.

Ovalle told the BBC that the Halcones, at least 400 or 500 by reports, were waiting at a crossing. Students pushed the first wave back, he said, and a second wave carrying M-1 rifles and other firearms opened fire. Víctor Guerra, another student leader, said he saw police get out of their vehicles to help the Halcones and hand them bamboo staves, and minutes later the shooting began. El Financiero's explainer says the attackers fired .45-calibre rounds and 30 M-2 carbines, and shouted "Viva el Che Guevara". Milenio, citing a document from the General Archive of the Nation, reports that a participant described the shooting starting around 18:30, some of it from below and some from rooftops. The same piece says about 850 soldiers dressed as civilians left a presidential guard unit that afternoon to blend in with the marchers. That claim rests on the archive documents Milenio cites, and other pages opened do not repeat it.

Colonel Alfonso Guarro, quoted in El Universal, put the public forces at 900 and the Halcones at 1,500. El Universal also cites the book Mexico Under Siege for the claim that federal police fired from their cars at those who had escaped the encirclement, and that police later supported the Halcones with tear gas.

Photographers and reporters were attacked. UNAM's Gaceta notes that, unlike in 1968, when agents visited newspapers to seize photographs, the effort to destroy images was made in the street itself, by Halcones attacking journalists. Images by independent photographers such as Armando Lenin Salgado circulated widely and became icons of the day.

The violence did not end with the dispersal of the march. Wounded students were taken to clinics including the Rubén Leñero hospital. Ovalle told the BBC that journalists, patients, doctors and nurses witnessed groups of Halcones entering and attacking students with firearms, which the press called the "finishing off" of the wounded. La Izquierda Diario says the same happened at the Cruz Verde hospital as well. El Universal, again citing Mexico Under Siege, says an attack was organised to recover injured Halcones from the hospital and that wounded students were dragged to Military Camp Number One.
content.h2: Denial and the count of the dead
content.p: On the night of the massacre, according to La Izquierda Diario, the capital's authorities said it had been a clash between students and that the Halcones did not exist. Martínez Domínguez called them an "urban legend", Milenio reports, citing a state historical institute. The attorney general's office first said some students had been armed and that snipers had fired on both marchers and police, according to the account BBC Mundo took from El Universal. El Financiero adds that the police even suggested that the Halcones were students who had turned on their own classmates. A week later, Díaz Escobar acknowledged that such a force existed, but he did not tie it to the massacre.

The number of dead became a second dispute. La Izquierda Diario says the press at first carried no more than 16 deaths, while there were reports of 30 bodies at one hospital; a list of 27 names and 13 unidentified people was published later, and the paper says the real figure is no lower than 120. El Universal's reconstruction records official sources acknowledging 11 dead, though it also reports a hawk who said he saw more than 30 dead, 100 wounded and 1,000 beaten. Vanguardia, citing official figures, gave at least 22 dead, many missing and around 50 injured, and said civil organisations raised the toll to 60. Prensa Libre, reproducing the BBC, said an exact count was never established but estimated roughly 30 dead. Several outlets, including El Financiero and Slate, repeat a figure of about 120.

Echeverría met reporters two days after the attack to apologise for the aggression against the press, Ovalle told the BBC. On 15 June Martínez Domínguez resigned as regent. U.S. diplomats judged that the resignation served Echeverría's own purposes: deputy chief of mission Jack Kubisch wrote that it was a move to establish undisputed presidential leadership and, perhaps, to find a high-level scapegoat. The embassy rejected a theory circulating in the press that Martínez Domínguez had staged the attack to weaken the president. It judged it unlikely that Echeverría "could not have forced the disbandment of the Halcones had he so desired" or was unaware of plans to repress the march. Its assessment said it was "hard to escape the conclusion that some deaths could have been expected". A State Department intelligence analysis of 17 June judged it a more likely account that Echeverría may have approved the group's use against the demonstrators.

La Izquierda Diario adds that the police chief and the federal attorney general, Julio Sánchez Vargas, left their posts in the following weeks, and that the Halcones were broken up and their training ground in San Juan de Aragón dismantled. An exhibition curated by Alberto del Castillo Troncoso, described by Gaceta UNAM, covers how, five days after the march, the ruling party organised a mass rally in the Zócalo to exonerate and glorify the president.

The same cables show Washington helping hide its part. On 17 June the embassy proposed letting the Mexican government know it was concerned about "irresponsible and unfounded attempts to connect us" with the events, and urged that no publicity be given to the police training. On 25 June Rabasa assured embassy officials that his government would do everything to prevent harmful publicity. By 22 December Ambassador McBride was writing that the government seemed to have no intention of ever issuing a full report on the attack.

For decades nobody answered for the killings. In the 2000s the federal government created a special prosecutor's office for past social and political movements, known as Femospp, headed by Ignacio Carrillo Prieto. The National Security Archive notes that Echeverría was under investigation by it, though it adds that the declassified documents did not provide a smoking gun.

BBC Mundo reports that Mexico's highest court held the crime of genocide had not expired for Echeverría and his interior secretary, Mario Moya Palencia. In July 2005, however, magistrate Herlinda Velasco Villavicencio of a federal appeals tribunal refused the arrest warrants the prosecutors sought. According to vLex, she found insufficient elements to call the events genocide, because the killings were not directed at a specific ethnic, racial or national group, and treated the events as a confrontation. The BBC adds that she saw simple homicide, which had been time-barred after more than 30 years. Slate says that Echeverría was later cleared of criminal responsibility because courts found no evidence to convict him. The sources opened do not agree on exact dates for that later ruling, so none is given here.

On the 50th anniversary, 10 June 2021, López Obrador opened his morning news conference with what he called a "sincere apology" in his capacity as representative of the Mexican state, together with a commitment that people who protest would never again be repressed, in a translation of his words quoted by El Financiero. He then met survivors and families of the disappeared of the Dirty War, Vanguardia reported. In 2020 the government had inaugurated a memorial for the massacre at the site of the former federal security agency, one of its "Memory Sites", where, El Universal says, young people were kidnapped and tortured.

The column reprinted by Mexico Solidarity Media in 2025 argues that no perpetrator or mastermind was ever investigated or punished. Mexico City's education minister, Rosaura Ruiz Gutiérrez, said, as El Universal reports, that no one had been charged or held responsible. Ovalle's reading is that 1971 was no repeat of 1968 but part of a counterinsurgency strategy of the Cold War years.
